# Backends and Runtimes: Nix, Podman, and Apptainer {#sec-backends}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*Using Singularity containers, developers can work in
reproducible environments of their choosing and design, and
these complete environments can easily be copied and
executed on other platforms.*

[Kurtzer, Sochat, and Bauer]{.smallcaps}, *Singularity:
Scientific Containers for Mobility of Compute* (2017)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

By the end of this chapter you will be able to take any
of three situations and name the one alternative to
Docker that fits, chosen by the constraint that actually
binds. The situations are a job a cluster's scheduler
refuses to run under Docker, a laboratory that has
declined to license Docker Desktop, and a reviewer who
will install nothing. The alternatives are Podman,
Apptainer, Nix, the conda family, and Binder, each a
route to the pinned-environment rung that
@sec-containers reaches with Docker.



::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 45 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-containers, for the Docker recipe,
the digest pin, and the dated snapshot that every
alternative in this chapter must match to count as reaching
the same rung. Also @sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder and
the capture-versus-validation vocabulary used throughout.
This chapter is marked optional in the one-quarter core
path (see the [Conventions](conventions.qmd) page); a
reader on that pace can skip it without losing the
ladder itself, which @sec-containers alone already
secures. No new statistics are introduced. R
knowledge assumed: calling a function with named arguments
and reading a short shell command; no new R idiom appears.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- explain why Docker is one route to the pinned-environment
  rung and not the only one?
- place a given tool, Podman, Apptainer, Nix via `rix`,
  conda, Binder, or a devcontainer, on the correct one of
  the three axes (runtime, backend, remote execution), and
  say what that axis does and does not change?
- run a container image under Podman or Apptainer, and read
  a small `default.nix` declaration produced by `rix`,
  without conflating what each one pins?
- given a concrete constraint, a cluster with no
  administrative rights, a Windows-only laboratory, a
  reviewer who installs nothing, name the one tool that
  fits, and state honestly which rung it reaches?

**Outline.** We begin with where the chapter sits on the
stack: the same two layers Docker captures, reached by a
different route. The orientation then introduces three
health scientists Docker cannot serve directly, and the
analyst's contribution follows, which is to diagnose the
binding constraint before picking a tool. The three axes
come next in turn. Axis one is a different runtime,
Podman or Apptainer, over the same image; axis two is a
different environment model, Nix, Guix, or conda,
without a container. Axis three is remote execution,
Binder or a devcontainer, off the analyst's machine. We
then choose among the alternatives with a comparison
table keyed to the binding constraint, and ask which
route would apply to this book's own compendium today.
The chapter closes with a worked example of one pinned
image and three destinations and a second, Apptainer under
Slurm on a cluster, followed by collaborating
with an LLM, exercises, a cheat sheet, and further
reading.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

This chapter captures nothing beyond what @sec-containers
already pinned. Its subject is reaching the identical rung
by a different road. @fig-stack-backends marks the same
two layers Docker's chapter captures, the operating system
and system libraries, and the R runtime. Here they are
reached by Podman, Apptainer, Nix, conda, or a remote
service instead of a locally built Docker image.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = c('Operating system, system libraries', 'R runtime'),
  title = 'Reaching the same pinned-environment rung by a different route')
```

## Orientation

In @sec-containers we reached the pinned-environment
level, L2 on the ladder of @sec-levels, by packaging an
analysis inside a Docker image. Such an image fixes the
operating system, the system libraries, and the R
interpreter that a lockfile alone leaves to chance. It is
easy to come away from that chapter believing that Docker
is reproducibility, that the two words name the same
thing. They do not. Docker is one instrument for reaching
L2, and a reader who mistakes the instrument for the goal
will be at a loss the first time Docker is unavailable,
unwanted, or forbidden.

Consider three health scientists who cannot simply follow
the Docker recipe of the previous chapter. The first runs
a large simulation study that must execute on a shared
university cluster, where the scheduler will not grant her
the administrative privileges that Docker's standard,
root-owned daemon requires. The
second works in a laboratory of Windows machines and a
pipeline that mixes R with Python, a combination that sits
awkwardly inside the Rocker images. The third has prepared
a teaching blog and wants a reviewer to re-run a single
post in a browser, installing nothing at all. Each needs
the pinned environment that L2 names; none of them can
obtain it in the ordinary Docker way. In this chapter we
shall see that the ladder does not depend on any one tool,
and how to choose among the alternatives by the
constraint at hand.

The framework this book uses organizes those
alternatives along three axes. The organization is
worth internalizing before any command is typed, because
it prevents the common error of treating every unfamiliar
tool as a special case. The first axis changes only the
runner: a different program runs the very same image, and
nothing about its pinning, its packages, or its base is
reinstalled. The second axis changes the environment model itself,
dispensing with the container and declaring the
environment directly, so that the pinned environment is
reached by a different mechanism. The third axis keeps the
container but moves it off the analyst's machine, into a
browser or a hosted service, so that the person
reproducing the work provides no environment of their own.
A tool belongs to exactly one axis, and knowing which axis
a tool occupies tells the analyst almost everything about
what it does and does not change. We take up the axes in
that order once the analyst's contribution has been
stated.

## The analyst's contribution

No tool in this chapter chooses itself. Three judgments
remain the analyst's, and they are the substance of the
chapter.

1. **Diagnose the constraint before selecting the
   tool.** The decisive question is usually which
   constraint is binding. Candidates include an absence
   of administrative rights on a cluster, an operating
   system, a mixed-language pipeline, a licensing term, a
   reviewer's patience, or a demand for maximum rigor.
   The analyst identifies the binding
   constraint first, and the constraint usually selects
   the axis, and often the tool.

2. **Locate each alternative on the correct axis.** A
   great deal of confusion in practice comes from
   treating Podman, Nix, and Binder as interchangeable
   answers to one question. They are answers to three
   different questions. The analyst who keeps the axes
   distinct will not, for example, expect Podman to solve
   a Windows-and-Python problem, nor expect Nix to spare
   a reviewer an installation.

3. **State the level each option actually reaches.** A
   Podman run of a digest-pinned image reaches L2 exactly
   as the Docker run did, and a Nix declaration reaches
   L2 without a container. A Binder session reaches L2
   for the duration of the session but pins nothing on
   the reviewer's own machine. The analyst reports the level
   honestly and never lets the novelty of a tool inflate
   the claim.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Runtime.** The program that runs a container image:
  Docker, Podman, or Apptainer. The runtime is
  interchangeable when the image is a standard OCI image.
- **OCI image.** An image built to the Open Container
  Initiative specification, the common format that
  Docker, Podman, and Apptainer can all consume. A Docker
  image is an OCI image.
- **Daemon.** A background system service that runs
  continuously with elevated privilege. A standard Docker
  installation relies on one; Podman and Apptainer do
  not, which is why they run without administrative
  rights. Docker also has a rootless mode, but its
  prerequisites are usually installed by an
  administrator, so on a shared cluster it is rarely
  available to an ordinary user.
- **Rootless.** Able to run under an ordinary user
  account, without the `root` superuser privilege. A
  requirement on shared clusters, where users are not
  administrators.
- **Backend.** The mechanism that supplies the
  environment. Docker is the container backend; Nix is a
  container-free backend that declares the environment
  directly.
- **Purely functional package manager.** A package
  manager, such as Nix, in which the installed result is
  treated as a function of the declared inputs, so that
  the same declaration, on the same platform, resolves
  to the same set of packages and dependencies.
- **Input-addressed.** Identified by a hash of the build
  inputs rather than by a mutable name, so that a
  reference cannot silently point at different content
  later.
- **SIF.** The Singularity Image Format, a single-file
  archive that Apptainer produces from an image, suitable
  for depositing alongside a compendium.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the third judgment

A biostatistician discovers Nix and begins describing her
project as 'fully reproducible using Nix,' before running
anything twice. Which of the analyst's three judgments has
she skipped?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The third: stating the level each option actually reaches.
Diagnosing the constraint and locating Nix on the correct
axis do not excuse the analyst from reporting the rung
honestly. At best Nix reaches L2, the pinned environment,
and only once the declaration has actually been run.
'Fully reproducible' overstates it because no rebuild has
been verified, which is this chapter's own honest-level
warning in miniature.
:::
:::

## Axis one: a different runtime over the same image

We begin with the cheapest of the three changes, because
it changes the least. The image built in @sec-containers,
pinned to its base by content digest and installing its
packages from a dated snapshot, is a standard OCI image.
Docker is the program that ran it, but the image does not
belong to Docker; any OCI-compatible runtime can run it.
Selecting a different runtime changes one
parameter. The base image, the digest pin, the dated
snapshot, and the lockfile all carry over unchanged, and
only the command that launches the container differs.

### Podman

Podman is a daemonless, rootless,
Docker-command-compatible runtime. Where Docker interposes
a background daemon running with elevated privilege,
Podman runs the container directly under the invoking
user's account. Its command-line interface is close
enough to Docker's that `podman run` stands in for
`docker run` in most cases:

```bash
$ podman build -t myproject .
$ podman run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/project myproject \
    Rscript -e 'source("analysis/run.R")'
```

Two properties recommend Podman to the health scientist.
The first is that, being daemonless and rootless, it runs
on a multi-user Linux machine where an analyst has no
administrative rights, a situation in which Docker's
daemon is often simply unavailable. The second concerns
licensing, and it catches many university users unawares.
Docker Desktop, the packaged Docker distribution for macOS
and Windows, is under its current terms not free for use
by larger commercial and institutional organizations, and
many universities fall within those terms. The terms do
carve out an exception for education, but institutions
differ on whether a given use qualifies. The point is
contested, which is why many institutions either license
Docker Desktop or avoid it. Podman carries no such
restriction. For an analyst whose institution has
declined to license Docker Desktop, Podman reaches the
same L2 environment, from the same image, at no
licensing cost.

### Apptainer

Apptainer, known until its move to the Linux Foundation as
Singularity, is the runtime built for high-performance
computing [@kurtzer2017]. Kurtzer and colleagues designed
it for the setting that defeats Docker on a cluster. It
runs unprivileged, integrating with the batch schedulers,
message-passing libraries, and graphics processors that
scientific clusters provide. A user with no
administrative rights can nonetheless run a containerized
analysis under the cluster's job system.

Two rules govern its use, and observing them keeps the
image pinning of @sec-containers intact. The first is that
an Apptainer image should be built from the
digest-pinned Docker image, never authored independently,
so that the build recipe stays pinned end to end. The SIF
file Apptainer produces gets its own content hash,
computed over the converted single-file format, not the
same bytes as the Docker digest. The two checksums
therefore differ. (Apptainer does not claim to preserve
the OCI digest identity into the SIF hash; what is
pinned is the input to the conversion, not the output's
checksum.) The build and a subsequent run look as
follows:

```bash
$ apptainer build env.sif \
    docker://ghcr.io/lab/env@sha256:9f2c...

$ apptainer exec env.sif \
    Rscript -e 'source("analysis/run.R")'
```

The second is that the single file Apptainer produces, the
SIF, is itself an archival artifact. Unlike a Docker image,
which lives in a layered local store, an Apptainer image is
one file that can be checksummed, deposited in a data
repository, and cited alongside the compendium. It is thus
both the thing that runs the analysis on the cluster and
the thing that is archived to let others run it later.
That is a convenient coincidence for the verification of
@sec-verification.

The expected pattern, and the one we recommend, is to
develop on the laptop with Docker or Podman and to run at
scale on the cluster with Apptainer, all from a single
image. Nothing is reinstalled for the cluster. Apptainer
repackages the pinned image into SIF, carrying the content
over from the same digest and converting only the format,
so the same pinned environment runs under a different
program.

This is the point at which the archetypes of @sec-compendium
begin to matter. A **simulation study**, which may need to
run thousands of replicates across the nodes of a cluster,
is the archetype that most naturally reaches for
Apptainer. The SIF file travels to the cluster, the
scheduler runs it unprivileged across many cores, and the
same file is later deposited as the archival record of
the environment. A
plain **data-analysis** project that runs comfortably on a
laptop has no such need and is better served by Docker or
Podman.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what changes with the runtime

An analyst has a Docker image pinned as
`FROM rocker/verse@sha256:...` with packages installed
from a dated snapshot. She switches from Docker to Podman
to avoid a licensing constraint. Which of the following
change: the base image, the pinned digest, the installed
package versions, the reproducibility level reached?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

None of them change. The runtime is a parameter
over the same OCI image. The base image, its digest, and
the package versions are all properties of the image, not
of the program that runs it, and the level reached is L2
in either case. Only the launching command differs
(`podman run` for `docker run`). This is why a
runtime swap is the cheapest of the three axes: it changes
the runner and nothing else.
:::
:::

## Axis two: a different environment model without a container

The second axis is a deeper change. Here we abandon the
container altogether and declare the environment directly,
reaching the pinned environment by a different mechanism.

### Nix and the rix front-end

Nix is a purely functional, input-addressed package
manager [@dolstra2004]. 'Purely functional' means that the
installed environment is a function of a declaration:
given the same declaration, Nix reconstructs the same
package set and dependency graph on the same platform,
at a later time. 'Input-addressed' means that every
built component is identified by a hash of its inputs.
A reference therefore cannot silently come to mean
something else, which is the mutable-tag failure we
guarded against in @sec-containers by pinning digests.
Input addressing fixes what goes into each build, not
that every build produces bit-identical output, and the
platform still matters. Dolstra, in the work that
introduced Nix, made this purely functional model the
organizing principle of the design, and that property is
what recommends Nix here.

The decisive fact for our purposes is that a single Nix
declaration fixes the R version, the R packages, and the
system libraries together. It therefore reaches the
pinned-environment level, L2, without a container at all.
This is why the ladder of @sec-levels speaks of 'a Docker
or Nix image'. Nix is not a supplement to the container,
in the way that `renv` is a supplement, but a peer of it,
an alternative road to the same rung.

The obstacle is that the Nix language is unfamiliar to
almost every biostatistician, and this is the dominant
reason it is not the default. The `rix` package removes
much of that obstacle by generating the Nix declaration
from R, in R idiom that a health scientist already knows
[@rodrigues2024rix]. Rodrigues and Baumann designed `rix`
so that the analyst writes a familiar R call and `rix`
writes the Nix:

```r
library(rix)

rix(
  r_ver = "4.4.1",
  r_pkgs = c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "targets"),
  system_pkgs = NULL,
  git_pkgs = NULL,
  ide = "rstudio",
  project_path = "."
)
```

That call produces a `default.nix` file, the declaration
that pins the environment. A reader need not master the
Nix language to recognize its shape; a minimal
`default.nix` reads, in outline, as follows:

```nix
let
  pkgs = import (fetchTarball
    "https://github.com/rstats-on-nix/nixpkgs/archive/<date>.tar.gz")
    {};
  rpkgs = with pkgs.rPackages; [ dplyr ggplot2 targets ];
  system_packages = with pkgs; [ R glibcLocales ];
in
pkgs.mkShell {
  buildInputs = [ rpkgs system_packages ];
}
```

The pinned `nixpkgs` snapshot, written as `<date>` above,
is the analogue of the base-image digest: it fixes the
set of package definitions from which the environment is
built. Current versions of `rix` point at a dated branch
of `rstats-on-nix/nixpkgs`, a fork of `nixpkgs` its
maintainers keep for R, rather than at a commit of the
main `NixOS/nixpkgs` repository. The generated
`fetchTarball` usually carries no `sha256` of the
archive. The pin is only as fixed as that dated
branch is kept; replacing the date with a full commit
hash, and adding the archive's `sha256`, makes it
stricter. Entering the environment is then a single
command, and no image is built:

```bash
$ nix-shell default.nix
```

Newer Nix workflows prefer a flake, a `flake.nix` paired
with a generated `flake.lock` that records the exact pin,
the direct analogue of `renv.lock`. Because flakes remain
behind an experimental flag in current Nix, the framework
tolerates both the classic `default.nix` and the flake
form, and the reader will encounter both in the wild.

Nix has trade-offs on both sides. On the plus side, it
delivers the entire environment pillar in one mechanism
and reaches L2 without the container machinery. Its
input-addressed builds pin the whole dependency graph
from one declaration, where Docker reaches a comparable
pin only through careful digest and snapshot
discipline. On the minus side, the Nix model is
alien to the audience. Although `rix` hides much of the
language, diagnosing a build that has failed still calls
for some Nix knowledge. The first
build is slow and consumes substantial disk. Nix is a host
prerequisite comparable to Docker, requiring Linux, macOS,
or the Windows Subsystem for Linux. And `rix` is young
enough that its own version must be pinned. These caveats
are the reason Nix is carried as an opt-in backend for the
analyst who wants maximum rigor, while `renv` with a
container remains the accessible default.

### Guix and the conda family

Two neighbors of Nix deserve mention, because a reader
will meet them and should know where they sit. GNU Guix is
Nix's close sibling, sharing the purely functional,
input-addressed model, with a smaller R ecosystem. For
the health scientist it is best understood simply as
Nix's relation, reaching the same rung by the same idea.

The conda family occupies a different middle ground, and
it answers two constraints the container route handles
awkwardly. Conda [@anaconda2023], with the faster resolver
`mamba` and the lockfile-oriented `pixi` [@pixi2024],
installs and runs directly on Windows, without the WSL2
or Hyper-V virtual machine a Docker (or Podman) image
requires there. This is a practical advantage, but not a
guarantee that any given package is available.
Conda-forge's Windows (`win-64`) build
coverage for R packages is narrower than its Linux
coverage. A pipeline that needs a package without a
`win-64` build therefore still needs a fallback, and
'reproduces on Windows' should be read as 'for the
packages that conda-forge actually ships there'. Conda
also spans R and Python in a single environment, so the
mixed-language analyst need not bridge two toolchains.
For a Windows-only laboratory running a pipeline that
mixes the two languages and whose packages are available
on `win-64`, this is a decisive practical advantage. The
cost is rigor: conda draws its packages from conda-forge
rather than from CRAN or the Posit Package Manager, and
it pins less strictly than Nix. It is a middle-ground
option, more reproducible than an unpinned install and
less exacting than Nix. It is the right choice when its
two native strengths, running directly on Windows and
spanning two languages, are the binding constraint and
the required packages are available there.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter describes as many as five routes to L2, the
pinned environment: Podman, Apptainer, Nix through `rix`,
a Binder session, or a devcontainer. Describing a route
is not taking it, and 'The cohort, continued' below
computes which, if any, the book's own compendium has
taken. Even a route taken is not verified until a clean
rebuild is compared against a recorded baseline within a
stated tolerance, which is what L3 requires. A
`default.nix` or a SIF file in a repository is a claim of
L2, no more, until
@sec-verification's baseline test has actually been run
(habit 7).
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: peer, not supplement

A `default.nix` generated by `rix` pins the R version, the
R packages, and the system libraries in one declaration,
with no Docker image anywhere. What rung does this reach,
and why does the chapter call Nix a peer of Docker rather
than a supplement to it?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

L2, the pinned-environment rung, exactly as Docker reaches
it. Nix is a peer rather than a supplement because the pin
is achieved directly, by declaration, with no container
format underneath it. There is no image for Nix to
supplement, in the way `renv` supplements an otherwise
unpinned project sitting inside a container.
:::
:::

## Axis three: remote execution

The third axis keeps the container but moves it off the
analyst's machine. The pinning is unchanged; what changes
is who runs it. This axis answers one limitation, the
learning curve and installation burden that a container
imposes on the person reproducing the work; the container
format itself is kept.

Binder runs a compendium's container in the browser, so
that a reviewer or reader installs nothing whatever
[@jupyter2018]. Jupyter's Binder service reads the
configuration files already present in a well-formed
compendium, builds the environment on a hosted server, and
serves it as an interactive session reached by a single
link. For the health scientist the appeal is that a
reviewer clicks a link and is inside the running
environment, with no Docker, no Nix, and no local
installation of any kind.

Two qualifications follow from how Binder works. First,
the service, through its `repo2docker` tool, builds its
own image from the repository's configuration files; it
does not pull a registry digest. A `.binder/` directory
of `install.R` and `runtime.txt` files yields
an environment resolved on Binder's server, not the
digest-pinned image of @sec-containers. Binder runs that
pinned image only when the configuration is a
`.binder/Dockerfile` whose `FROM` line names the digest,
and the image must also serve Jupyter, which a
`rocker/binder` base provides, with
`jupyter-rsession-proxy` for RStudio. Second, the public
service limits each session's memory and lifetime. The
honest level is then L2 for the life of the session, and
only when the image is the pinned one. Nothing is pinned
on the reviewer's own machine, and the session does not
persist. Binder suits demonstration and review; it is not
an archival guarantee.

Development containers, and the hosted Codespaces service
built on them, bring the same pinned environment into an
editor rather than a browser [@devcontainers]. A
`.devcontainer/` configuration in the compendium describes
the environment, and a compatible editor or the Codespaces
service builds and opens it. A collaborator then edits
and runs inside the pinned environment without assembling
it locally. The principle is the same presence-driven one
we have met throughout: the configuration file's existence
drives the automated build.

Here again the archetype guides the choice. A **blog** or a
**manuscript** archetype, whose whole purpose is to be read
and its results inspected by others, benefits most from
browser execution. A reader of a teaching post, or a
reviewer of a manuscript, re-runs the analysis in Binder
with nothing to install, which is the low-friction path
such archetypes want. A blog that renders many posts
gains the most, since each post becomes independently
re-runnable by a reader at a link. A **simulation**
archetype, by contrast, gains little from browser execution and much
from the cluster, which is the Apptainer story of the first
axis. The reproducibility machinery is the same across all
archetypes; the archetype decides only how it is delivered.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what a Binder session pins

A `.binder/` configuration lets a reviewer run a
compendium's main figure in a browser with nothing
installed. Does the session pin anything on the reviewer's
own machine? What rung does the session itself reach, and
for how long?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No; the environment lives entirely on Binder's hosted
server, and nothing is pinned on the reviewer's machine. The
session reaches L2 for as long as it runs only if the
configuration is a `.binder/Dockerfile` built `FROM` the
compendium's digest-pinned image. A configuration of
`install.R` and `runtime.txt` files makes Binder resolve
its own environment, which is not the compendium's pin.
Even then the pin does not persist once the
session ends, which is why Binder serves demonstration and review
rather than archiving.
:::
:::

## Choosing among the alternatives

With the three axes laid out, the governing question, as
the analyst's first contribution insisted, is which
constraint binds. We answer it by setting the guidance
beside a compact comparison, generated at build time from
the same tibble that a reader could inspect directly.


::: {#tbl-backends .cell tbl-cap='Backends and runtimes for reaching the pinned environment, by axis'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

comparison <- tibble(
  name = c(
    "Docker", "Podman", "Apptainer",
    "Nix (via rix)", "Guix", "conda / pixi",
    "Binder", "Devcontainer / Codespaces"
  ),
  axis = c(
    "runtime", "runtime", "runtime",
    "backend", "backend", "backend",
    "remote", "remote"
  ),
  pins = c(
    "the image (OS, R, libraries)",
    "the image (OS, R, libraries)",
    "the image, as one SIF file",
    "R, packages, system libraries",
    "R, packages, system libraries",
    "R and Python packages, less strictly",
    "the image (server-side, per session)",
    "the image (in the editor)"
  ),
  container = c(
    "yes", "yes", "yes",
    "no", "no", "no",
```

|:-------------------------|:-------|:------------------------------------|:------------|:-----------------------------------------|

|Podman                    |runtime |the image (OS, R, libraries)         |yes          |licensing constraint; rootless Linux      |
|Apptainer                 |runtime |the image, as one SIF file           |yes          |an HPC cluster; archival SIF              |

:::
:::


Read as guidance, the table resolves into a short set of
recommendations, each keyed to a binding constraint. When
the destination is an **HPC cluster** and the analyst has
no administrative rights, the choice is Apptainer, built
from the same digest-pinned image and run under the
scheduler. The SIF file then doubles as the archival
deposit. When the setting is a **Windows-only laboratory**,
or the pipeline **mixes R and Python**, the choice is the
conda family, `pixi` in particular. It reproduces natively
on Windows and spans both languages at the cost of strict
pinning. When a **reviewer must install nothing**,
the choice is Binder, which serves the running environment
in a browser for the life of a session. When the project
demands **maximum rigor** and the team can absorb the
learning curve, the choice is Nix through `rix`, whose
input-addressed builds reach L2 without a container. And
when the obstacle is a **licensing constraint**, an
institution that has not licensed Docker
Desktop, the choice is Podman. Podman reaches the
identical L2 environment from the identical image at no
licensing cost. The default, for the analyst under none of these
constraints, remains Docker with `renv`, the composition of
@sec-containers.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Worked example

To make the axes concrete, consider a single research
group with one image and three destinations, which is a
common situation once a project matures. The group has
built a pinned image for a cohort-analysis compendium,
`ghcr.io/lab/cohort-env`, resolved to an immutable digest.

On the analyst's own laptop, at an institution that has
declined to license Docker Desktop, the image runs under
Podman with no change to the image and no licensing cost:

```bash
$ podman run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/project \
    ghcr.io/lab/cohort-env@sha256:9f2c... \
    Rscript -e 'source("analysis/run.R")'
```

When a sensitivity analysis must be repeated across many
simulated cohorts, the work moves to the university
cluster. The analyst builds a SIF from the same digest and
submits it to the scheduler. Nothing is rebuilt, and the
image contents are the same ones pinned on the laptop,
because the SIF was built from that one digest and not
reauthored. The SIF pins the recipe; it does not control
what the cluster passes into the run.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

By default, Apptainer binds the user's `$HOME` as a
read-write mount and passes host environment variables
through into the container [@apptainer_bind]. A stray
`R_LIBS_USER` or locale variable set on the cluster login
node can therefore still leak into execution, even though
the image itself did not change. The `--cleanenv` flag drops the
inherited environment variables, and only those. The
host `$HOME` stays mounted, and with it any
`~/.Rprofile`, `~/.Renviron`, and user package library
under `~/R`, which R inside the container still reads.
A verified run therefore adds `--no-home`, binds only
the project directory with `--bind "$PWD"`, and starts R
with `--vanilla` so that no startup file is read. The
combination `--containall --bind "$PWD" --pwd "$PWD"`
isolates the same things; without `--pwd` it starts the
job in the container's home directory, where relative
paths such as `analysis/simulate.R` no longer resolve.
:::

```bash
$ apptainer build cohort-env.sif \
    docker://ghcr.io/lab/cohort-env@sha256:9f2c...

$ apptainer exec --cleanenv --no-home --bind "$PWD" \
    cohort-env.sif \
    Rscript --vanilla -e 'source("analysis/simulate.R")'
```

Finally, when the paper is submitted, a reviewer wishes to
re-run the principal figure without installing anything.
The compendium carries a one-line `.binder/Dockerfile`
that starts from the same digest. This works only because
the group built `cohort-env` on a `rocker/binder` base,
so the image already serves Jupyter and RStudio:

```dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/lab/cohort-env@sha256:9f2c...
```

Binder builds from that file on a hosted server and
serves the environment in the browser, reached by a
single link in the cover letter. A `.binder/` of
`install.R` and `runtime.txt` would instead make Binder
resolve an environment of its own, which is not the pin
the laptop and the cluster share.

The three destinations used three tools, drawn from two of
the three axes, and one image throughout. The pinning was
done once, in @sec-containers; this chapter merely ran it
in three places. Had the group instead chosen Nix from the outset,
the image would have been replaced by a `default.nix`, and
the laptop and cluster runs would have entered the
environment through `nix-shell` rather than a runtime.
The discipline, one pinned declaration exercised in several
places, would have been identical.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what made three destinations cheap

The research group never touches its Dockerfile again
after the original build, across the laptop, the cluster,
and the Binder deposit. What single fact about the three
axes makes that possible?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

All three destinations operate on, or around, the same
pinned recipe, and none reinstalls it. Axis one swaps
only the program that runs the image (Podman, Apptainer),
and axis three moves where that same image runs (a hosted
server). Neither axis asks what packages or base layer
the image contains. Only switching to axis two, replacing
the image with a Nix declaration, would have required
redoing the pin itself, because then there is no image left
to carry forward.
:::
:::

## An HPC worked example: Apptainer under Slurm

This section is supplementary to an already-optional
chapter, and the reader may skip it freely if the cluster
destination above was enough. It extends that story with the submission
mechanics a real cluster imposes, because knowing that
Apptainer is the right tool does not by itself tell an
analyst how a job reaches the scheduler.

Three realities of a shared cluster shape the script below.
First, the analyst has no administrative rights on any
node. As explained above, Apptainer runs unprivileged, so a
job submitted under the analyst's own account can still
execute a containerized analysis, and that is why it is the
standard choice on shared clusters. Second, the SIF file
typically sits on a shared, read-only filesystem mounted
on every compute node. The image is built once, usually
on a login node or a separate build host with outbound
network access, since compute nodes are often firewalled
from the registry the image is pulled from. Third, and most consequentially, the analyst cannot
install anything at the operating-system level once that
image is built and placed on the shared filesystem. There
is no `apt install` to fall back on from inside a running
job. On a cluster, then, the pinning discipline of
@sec-containers is a requirement: the SIF
built from the digest-pinned image is the only environment
the job will ever see, for the life of the allocation.

A minimal submission script for the cohort-analysis image
introduced in the worked example above looks like this:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=cohort-analysis
#SBATCH --partition=general
#SBATCH --time=02:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=8G
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --array=1-100
#SBATCH --output=cohort-analysis-%A_%a.log

apptainer exec --cleanenv --no-home --bind "$PWD" \
    --env SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID="$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID" \
    --env SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK="$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK" \
    /shared/images/cohort-env.sif \
    Rscript --vanilla -e 'source("analysis/simulate.R")'
```

The `#SBATCH` lines are directives Slurm's `sbatch` command
reads out of the script before any shell code runs. They
specify the partition to queue on, a wall-clock time
limit, a memory reservation, a core count, an array of
100 tasks (one per simulated replicate set), and a
destination for each task's combined output. In the
output name, `%A` is substituted for the array's job ID
and `%a` for the task's index. An analyst with access to
a compliant cluster would submit the script with `sbatch
run-cohort.sh`.

The `apptainer exec` line carries the same flags met in
the Pitfall above, applied here to a batch job. Slurm's
own job environment carries login-node variables, module
loads, and whatever a cluster's site-wide profile sets,
into the job by default. This is the batch-system version
of the leakage the Pitfall described for an interactive
shell. `--cleanenv` drops those variables, `--no-home`
keeps the host home directory and its R startup files
and user library out of the container, `--bind "$PWD"`
exposes the project directory the job was submitted
from, and `--vanilla` stops R reading any startup file.
The job then runs against the image's own pinned packages
and nothing the cluster happened to load on the
analyst's behalf. Because `--cleanenv` also strips the
`SLURM_*` variables, the script passes back the two the
analysis needs with `--env`. `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` tells
`simulate.R` which replicate set to run, and should also
choose its seed. `SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` tells it how many
cores it was granted. The image of @sec-containers pins
`OMP_NUM_THREADS` and `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` to 1, so the
four requested cores are used only if the script itself
runs R-level parallel work across that count; a script
that does not should request one core.

This script's `#SBATCH` directive syntax is inspected
against standard Slurm usage, not verified end to end.
No Slurm cluster was available to actually submit it. The
script should be treated as an illustrative
template to adapt to a given site's partition names and
resource limits, not as a script copied and run
unexamined.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the script does and does not pin

A colleague asks why the submission script above needs
`--cleanenv` when the SIF file was already built from a
digest-pinned image. What would leak into the job without
it, and what does the flag not protect against?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Without `--cleanenv`, Slurm's job environment would pass
through into the container alongside the pinned image,
exactly as it would in an interactive Apptainer session.
That environment includes variables a cluster's
login-node profile or a loaded module sets, such as a
stray `R_LIBS_USER` or a locale setting. The flag clears
those variables and nothing else. It does not isolate the
host `$HOME`, which Apptainer still mounts, so a
`~/.Rprofile`, a `~/.Renviron`, or a user library under
`~/R` would still reach R; that takes `--no-home` (or
`--containall`) and `Rscript --vanilla`, as the script
uses. It also strips the `SLURM_*` variables the job may
need, which is why the script passes them back with
`--env`. None of these flags touches the image's own
pinned contents, which were already fixed when the SIF
was built from the digest. A job
that fails only without `--cleanenv`, and succeeds with it,
is failing because of something outside the image, not
inside it.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for the mechanics
of this chapter and a poor judge of its trade-offs. The
commands and recipes it helps with need no data, but they
can name it, and the prompts should keep them from doing
so.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

One rule comes first (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable records, or data
held under a data use agreement, nor outputs derived from
them, into a model or a coding agent unless three conditions
all hold. The institution has approved that endpoint for
that class of data. The IRB protocol and the consent permit
the processing. The data use agreement, or the provider's
terms, permits it. If any of the three is unclear, the
answer is no.

The third condition is the one most often missed.
Institutional approval of a tool does not override the terms
under which a data provider released the data. NIH, for
example, treats sharing controlled-access data with
third-party generative AI tools through prompts as a breach
of the data use certification, and a model trained on such
data as a derivative that may not be distributed without
approval [@nihgenai2025].

Describe the structure instead: the column names and types,
or a small synthetic example generated from the data
dictionary, never edited from real rows. A coding agent sees
whatever files are in its working tree, so run it in a
checkout or container where the real data is not mounted.

An agent also acts, so confine it to a branch and keep merges,
pushes, and deposits for yourself (@sec-llm-delegate).
:::


Any host path that names a site, study, or participant
should be replaced with a placeholder before a command
is pasted. For the commands of this chapter, what a
coding agent can see runs through the bind mount:
whatever `-v` or `--bind` names is visible to an agent
that runs them. The following triples show where each
stands.

**Prompt.** 'Convert this `docker run` command to the
equivalent Podman and Apptainer commands, preserving the
bind mount and the digest-pinned image.'

*Watch for.* Check that the `--platform` flag survives,
that the Apptainer bind syntax is the real one and not an
invented `--volume` form, and that the digest, not a
mutable tag, was translated. A tag in place of the digest
silently undoes the pin.

*Verification.* Run the translated command and confirm
it executes the analysis; confirm the digest, not a tag,
appears in the Apptainer `docker://` reference; and
confirm the bind mount exposes the working tree as
expected.

*A better prompt.* 'Convert the attached `docker run`
command, which uses `--platform linux/amd64`, a digest-pinned
image, and one bind mount of the working tree, to Podman
and to Apptainer. Keep the digest, the platform, and the
mount target unchanged, and add no other mounts. For each
command, give the check that shows which image digest ran
and which host directory the container could see.'

**Prompt.** 'Write a `rix::rix()` call that pins R 4.4.1
with dplyr, ggplot2, and targets, producing a
`default.nix`.'

*Watch for.* Check that the answer is the `rix` call
requested rather than hand-written raw Nix, that the
`nixpkgs` revision, the whole point of the pin, is
present, and that every package exists under
`pkgs.rPackages`.

*Verification.* Run the `rix` call, inspect the generated
`default.nix` for a concrete pinned revision, and enter
the environment with `nix-shell` to confirm the packages
load. A declaration that builds is the only evidence that
counts.

**Prompt.** 'My analysis mixes R and Python and my lab uses
Windows. Should I use Nix, Podman, or conda?'

*Watch for.* Check whether the recommendation follows the
constraint or a tool's general reputation, and whether it
overstates a tool's rigor, for example by presenting
conda as reaching the same level as Nix.

*Verification.* Check the recommendation against the
binding constraint: mixed languages on Windows point to
the conda family, whatever a tool's general reputation.
The analyst, not the model, owns the honest statement of
the level reached.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. The first
three are hands-on and their outputs will vary by machine;
the boxes record the reasoning and the expected shape of the
result.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

```bash
podman run --rm -v "$PWD":/project -w /project \
  <image>@sha256:... Rscript analysis/run.R
```

The container starts and the analysis runs, with no
rebuild, because Podman consumes the same OCI image format
Docker produces. The command differs only in its first
word.

**Why the level is unchanged.** The reproducibility level
is a property of what is *captured*, and the image is the
capture. The base image, its digest, the installed package
versions, and the determinism variables are all properties
of the image, not of the program that launches it.
Swapping the launcher therefore changes nothing that the
ladder grades. The analysis sits at L2 under either runtime.

This is the sense in which the runtime is the cheapest of
the three axes: it changes the runner and nothing else.
One caveat: rootless Podman handles file ownership on
bind mounts differently from Docker, so the *mechanics*
of the mount may need adjusting even though the
environment inside does not change.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

```bash
apptainer build analysis.sif docker://<image>@sha256:...
sha256sum analysis.sif
```

The build converts the OCI image into a single SIF file.
The checksum is a hash of that file.

**How one file serves both purposes.** As a cluster
runtime, the SIF needs no daemon and no root, which is
what makes it acceptable on a shared HPC system where the
user is not an administrator. The scheduler runs
`apptainer exec analysis.sif ...` directly. As an
archival deposit, the SIF is a single immutable file with
a checksum, which is the shape an archive wants. It can
be uploaded to a repository, assigned a DOI, and verified
on download by rehashing.

The property that unifies the two roles is that a SIF is a
file rather than a service. A Docker image lives in a
daemon's storage and is addressed by a name that a
registry must resolve. A SIF, by contrast, is bytes on
disk that can be copied, hashed, and deposited like any
other artifact.
That is why the chapter treats it as the archival form of
a container.

Two qualifications apply. The SIF is opaque: it records
the environment without recording how it was made, so the
Dockerfile remains the source of truth and the SIF is the
built product. And SIF files are large, often several
gigabytes, which some archives will not accept.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

```r
rix::rix(
  r_ver = '4.4.0',
  r_pkgs = c('dplyr', 'ggplot2', 'targets'),
  project_path = '.'
)
```

The pinned `nixpkgs` snapshot appears near the top of the
generated `default.nix`, in the `fetchTarball` expression
that imports `nixpkgs`. In current versions of `rix` it is
a dated branch of the `rstats-on-nix/nixpkgs` fork, a URL
ending in a date such as `2024-10-01.tar.gz`, and it
usually carries no `sha256` of the fetched archive. Older
versions of `rix`, and hand-written declarations, may
instead name a commit of `NixOS/nixpkgs`. Whichever you
find, a full commit hash with a `sha256` is the stricter
pin, and a date is only as fixed as its branch is kept.

**What would change if the revision were altered.**
Essentially everything below the R packages, and some of
the packages too. The `nixpkgs` revision determines the
entire dependency graph. That graph includes the R
version itself, the C and Fortran compilers used to build
it, the BLAS and LAPACK implementations, every system
library, and the versions of the R packages available at
that revision. Moving the revision moves all of them
together.

This property is what makes Nix interesting for
reproducibility. The revision is a single value that pins
the whole stack from the system libraries upward. By
contrast, a lockfile pins only the R packages, and a
container pins a built artifact rather than a recipe for
one. It is also the property that
makes Nix unforgiving, since there is no way to move one
component without moving the revision, and moving the
revision moves everything.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

**(a) A laboratory forbidden from licensing Docker
Desktop.** Axis one, a different runtime over the same
image: Podman. The images, the digests, and the recipes
are unchanged, so the constraint is met at the cost of
changing one word in the launch command.

**(b) A reviewer who must run a figure with no local
installation.** Axis three, remote execution: Binder,
which builds the environment from the repository and
serves it in a browser for the session. The reviewer
installs nothing.

**(c) A simulation study destined for a shared cluster.**
Axis one again, but a different tool: Apptainer, because
a shared cluster will not grant the root daemon a
standard Docker installation requires. The SIF also
doubles as the archival record.

**(d) A Windows-only pipeline mixing R and Python.** Axis
two, a different environment model: the conda family, and
`pixi` in particular, which reproduces natively on Windows
and spans both languages without a container.

No single tool answers all four, and each constraint
selects an *axis* before it selects a tool.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

A serviceable reply:

> Nix pins the whole stack from the system libraries
> upward, and does it from a recipe rather than a built
> artifact, so it reaches L2 as cleanly as a container
> does and arguably more transparently. What it does not

> and L3 is verification: it needs evidence that the
> analysis was rebuilt from the pinned definition and
> regenerated its recorded outputs within a stated
> tolerance, which a baseline test establishes and Nix
> does not.

The correction to make is the level claim, not the tool
choice. 'Fully reproducible' is the phrase that overstates,
and it overstates in the direction this book cares about:
it asserts verification that has not been performed. The
colleague is right that Nix is a strong capture mechanism
and right to prefer it if they value a declarative recipe;
they are wrong that capture is the whole ladder.

Worth adding if the conversation continues: Nix pins more
of the stack than a lockfile and does not pin the hardware
or the intrinsic non-determinism, so even the capture claim
has a ceiling.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**The simulation archetype** most naturally uses Apptainer
on a scheduler. Its work is many independent replicates,
which suits a cluster, and a cluster will not run a root
daemon. The SIF is built once from the digest-pinned image
and dispatched to every node.

**The blog archetype** most naturally uses remote
execution: Binder, if readers are to run the posts
themselves. Its audience is on the web, and each post is
small enough for a browser session. The render on every
push is a separate matter, the continuous integration of
@sec-verification, which is not one of this chapter's
three axes.

**Why the pinning is nonetheless identical.** Both are
built from the same compendium machinery: the same
digest-pinned base image, the same dated snapshot, the
same restored lockfile, the same determinism variables.
The SIF is a conversion of that image, not a different
environment, and a Binder session reaches the same pin
only when its `.binder/Dockerfile` starts from that
digest.
Neither archetype changes what is captured; they differ
only in where the captured environment is executed and by
what program.

The backends and runtimes are an axis of *delivery*, and the
reproducibility level is set on an axis of *capture*. A
simulation on a cluster and a blog in Binder can sit on
exactly the same rung, because they are running the same
pinned thing in different places.
:::

## Exercise 8

(a)

```bash
apptainer build cohort-env.sif \
  docker://rocker/r-ver@sha256:<the digest from Chapter 7>
```

(b) The SIF's checksum is computed over the bytes of the
converted single-file archive, not over the Docker image's
layers. Converting a pinned input into a different format
therefore produces a different set of bytes, and so a
different hash, even though the input digest was pinned.
The SIF also embeds build metadata, so two conversions of
the same digest need not hash alike either.
What is pinned is the *input* to the conversion; the SIF's
own checksum is evidence about the *output*, and the two
need not, and do not, match.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-backends}

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `podman run ...` | Daemonless, rootless substitute for `docker run`; same OCI image, same digest, same L2. |
| `apptainer build x.sif docker://img@sha256:...` | Converts a digest-pinned OCI image into one archival SIF file. |
| `apptainer exec --cleanenv --no-home --bind "$PWD" x.sif Rscript --vanilla ...` | Runs the SIF with host environment variables cleared, the host `$HOME` unmounted, only the project directory bound, and no R startup file read; `--cleanenv` alone clears variables only (see the Pitfall above). |
| `rix::rix(r_ver=, r_pkgs=, project_path=)` | Generates a `default.nix` pinning R, packages, and system libraries together. |
| `nix-shell default.nix` | Enters the Nix-declared environment; no image is built. |
| `.binder/Dockerfile` | Lets Binder serve the compendium's pinned image in a browser, per session, when its `FROM` line names the digest; `install.R` and `runtime.txt` make Binder resolve its own environment instead. |
| `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` | Lets an editor or Codespaces open the pinned environment directly. |
| Rule of thumb | Diagnose the binding constraint first; it selects the axis, and usually the tool. |
| Rule of thumb | A runtime swap (axis one) changes the runner only; the image, digest, and packages carry over unchanged. |
| Habit 2 | Pin what you ran: the `nixpkgs` revision and the image digest are the same idea on two axes. |
| Habit 7 | A `default.nix` or a SIF is a capture claim only, until @sec-verification's baseline test has run. |

## Further reading

The high-performance-computing runtime is described by its
authors in @kurtzer2017, which sets out the unprivileged,
scheduler-integrated design and the single-file image
format that make Apptainer, formerly Singularity, the
natural cluster companion to a Docker workflow.

The foundational account of the purely functional,
input-addressed model is @dolstra2004. The R front-end
that makes it approachable for the health scientist is
documented in @rodrigues2024rix, whose `rix` package
generates the Nix declaration from ordinary R code.

For the conda family as a middle-ground backend, we have
two references: the reference documentation of the conda
ecosystem [@anaconda2023] and that of the
lockfile-oriented `pixi` [@pixi2024]. Together they
describe the native-Windows and mixed-language
reproduction that distinguishes it from the container
route.

The remote-execution axis is introduced by @jupyter2018,
whose Binder service runs a compendium's container in the
browser, and by the development-containers specification
[@devcontainers], which brings the same environment into an
editor. Both rest on the presence-driven principle, a
configuration file's existence driving an automated build,
that recurs throughout this book and is developed in
@sec-verification.

The container backend against which all of these are
alternatives is developed in @sec-containers, and the
ladder of levels that lets us state honestly what each of
them reaches is @sec-levels.
